findings.title: New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a ServiceLoader SPI, but order() was added as an abstract method instead of a default method. Any existing out-of-tree or downstream implementation compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration calls CryptoProvider::order during provider detection, and source implementations or mocks will no longer compile. Adding a default implementation, for example returning 0, would preserve compatibility while allowing built-in providers to declare higher precedence.

findings.title: Equal provider orders make selection nondeterministic and silently ignore conflicting providers
findings.body: Providers are now sorted only by order(), while DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. If more than one of them is accidentally present, the previous explicit 'multiple crypto providers' error is replaced by silently choosing whichever ServiceLoader/classpath ordering returns first. This can silently select the non-FIPS provider in a deployment expecting FIPS, and ServiceLoader instantiation can already have run the other providers' constructors and their global Java Security provider registration side effects. Built-in providers need distinct priorities or ties at the highest order should remain an error.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider instead of BouncyCastle
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract for getBouncyCastleProvider() is to return the BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns the provider backing a newly created default-type KeyStore, typically the SUN provider for PKCS12. Callers that use the returned provider for BouncyCastle-specific algorithms, keystore types, or provider-name checks will therefore fail or misidentify the active crypto mode. It should return an actual BouncyCastle provider, return null as the Elytron provider does when BouncyCastle is unavailable, or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unsupported methods in this class.

findings.title: ES384 and ES512 tests reuse a default-curve key and only assert round-trip identity
findings.body: The test creates one EC key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so it does not create P-384 or P-521 keys for ES384/ES512. It then only asserts that concatenated R/S converted to DER and back equals the padded concatenated value, without verifying the DER signature against the public key, comparing it with the original JCA DER signature, or checking the expected curve-specific lengths. Defects in 48/66-byte R/S handling, leading-zero stripping, or the long-form DER length needed for real ES512 signatures can therefore pass undetected. Each algorithm should generate a key on its corresponding curve and verify the reconverted DER signature.

findings.title: Malformed zero-length ASN.1 integer escapes as NumberFormatException instead of IOException
findings.body: readInteger() passes the decoded byte array directly to new BigInteger(bytes). A malformed DER integer with length 0 makes that constructor throw NumberFormatException, although callers such as asn1derToConcatenatedRS() are written to handle IOException for invalid signatures. Invalid input can consequently abort processing with an unchecked exception instead of the declared, handled error type. Zero-length and otherwise invalid integer encodings should be rejected with IOException before constructing the BigInteger.
